Since the fiber fabrication conditions were able to be successfully replicated after determining that dichloromethane was the most appropriate solvent for the core solution, the silica substrate was changed from SBA-15 to the high pore volume mesoporous silica (MS11). The batch of fibers shown in Figure 26a were spun using the same fiber fabrication conditions as the batch in Figure 25, with the only difference being a higher concentration of silica in the core solution (increased from 0.3 to 0.4 g per 10 mL). After washing, the fibers were imaged (Figure 26b) to ensure that the core-shell structure was maintained, and the silica was not extracted from the fibers during the washing process. This batch of fibers had the desired structure, so they were prepared with the PA- coated MS11 sorbents to be tested for their DAC performance. Figure 26. Since PEF with loaded mesoporous silica were able to be successfully replicated with the desired loading, they were then prepared with the optimized PA-coated sorbents for testing under DAC conditions. 3.3. DAC Performance of Hierarchical Nanoporous Capsules Based on systematic optimization, sample T2-0.5x was selected for comprehensive DAC performance evaluation under both controlled simulated conditions and authentic atmospheric conditions to validate practical deployment readiness. Figure 27a shows the cycling stability under simulated dry DAC conditions (400 ppm CO /N , 30°C adsorption for 8 hours, 100°C desorption 2 2 30 a a b b with 10-minute hold). The coated T2-0.5x material demonstrated exceptional stability over 15 consecutive cycles with capacity remaining constant at 0.97 ± 0.01 mmol/g throughout the entire cycling test. The consistent capacity across all 15 cycles confirms that the coating maintains its integrity and protective function under realistic thermal cycling that mimics field deployment, where minimizing regeneration time and energy is economically important. The absolute capacity under DAC conditions (0.97 mmol/g) is lower than under accelerated cycling at 15% CO (Figure 2 18) due to the thermodynamic limitation of capturing CO from dilute streams. At 400 ppm (0.04% 2 CO ), the driving force for adsorption is much lower than at 15% CO , resulting in incomplete 2 2 saturation of all available amine sites even after 8 h of exposure. This behavior is typical for amine sorbents and reflects the fundamental challenge of DAC where low CO concentrations limit 2 achievable working capacities. The optimized HNC was also tested for Dac under humid conditions (Figure 27b) and showed an initial CO capacity of 3.1 mmol/g (calculated by 2 integrating the breakthrough curves).
